query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermo‐mechanical processing route that refines the inherited eutectic lamellar structure into a hierarchically heterogeneous ultrafine-duplex microstructure will simultaneously increase both the strength and ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a coarse, lamellar dual-phase (soft FCC + hard BCC/B2) structure with typical cast defects.
generation.intervention: Apply severe cold rolling followed by a controlled annealing treatment to induce grain and lamella refinement, thereby engineering a hierarchical ultrafine-duplex lamellar microstructure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing (and/or quasi-static strain rate ~10^−3 s^−1) in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined hierarchical lamellar architecture with increased interphase boundary density and a heterogeneous microstructure that promotes both dislocation storage and effective strain distribution.
generation.mechanism: The severe deformation (cold rolling) increases dislocation density and promotes the formation of a high density of fine lamellar regions. Subsequent annealing activates recovery and partial recrystallization which refines grain/lamella sizes and distributes residual stresses. This microstructural evolution enhances strain hardening by providing abundant barriers to dislocation motion while the heterogeneous lamellar record helps to arrest microcrack propagation, leading to a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as-cast microstructure, the processed alloy is expected to show a significant increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths while retaining or modestly improving ductility (e.g., improvements on the order of 10–20% in both properties, acknowledging uncertainty in precise values).
generation.baseline: The cast eutectic HEA with its coarser, original lamellar eutectic microstructure.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted for eutectic HEAs featuring inherent dual-phase lamellar structures; it may not be directly applicable to single-phase HEAs or eutectics with markedly different phase chemistries.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement and the precise processing parameters required to achieve the optimal hierarchical structure are not fully determined, and the effect might vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set in the as-cast state and another set that undergoes severe cold rolling followed by controlled annealing to refine the lamellar microstructure. Perform identical tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (optical/SEM/TEM) to confirm ultrafine hierarchical lamellar formation.
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation) from tensile tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed specimens do not exhibit simultaneous increases in both yield strength and ductility (i.e. if improvements in one property come at the expense of the other or if there is no statistically significant enhancement relative to the as-cast baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
